title: The Drought and the Lying Prophets
summary: A severe drought grips Judah: cisterns are empty, the ground is cracked, and even wild animals abandon their young. Jeremiah prays for the people, confessing their sin and appealing to God's name, but God refuses to accept their fasting and offerings and again forbids the prophet to intercede. When Jeremiah protests that other prophets are promising peace, God condemns them as liars, and the chapter ends with the prophet's tears and a second anguished prayer that clings to God as the only one who sends rain.
story: Chapter 14 opens a section (14:1 to 15:9) built around a real disaster. Jeremiah has warned that God's covenant curses are coming; drought was one of them, named in Deuteronomy 28:23-24. Now the land itself is suffering. The chapter is a conversation: the people (or Jeremiah speaking for them) pray, God answers, the prophet argues, God answers again. It shows Jeremiah caught between his people and his God, loving both, and it brings into the open a conflict that will run through the rest of the book: Jeremiah's word of judgment against the popular prophets who promised that everything would be fine.
historical:
The chapter doesn't say when the drought happened, and no outside record fixes it. Judah was a land of rain-fed farming, with no great river like Egypt's Nile or Mesopotamia's Tigris and Euphrates to irrigate it, so failed winter rains meant failed harvests and, in time, famine. Jerusalem's water supply depended on springs and on cisterns, chambers cut into the rock and plastered to collect runoff. When the rains failed, cisterns stood empty.

The prophets who promised "lasting peace in this place" (verse 13) were real and influential. Jeremiah's conflict with them grows through the book, most memorably in his confrontation with Hananiah in chapter 28. They probably drew on a genuine tradition, the promise that God had chosen Zion and would defend it, which had seemed to be confirmed when Jerusalem survived the Assyrian siege of 701 BC in Hezekiah's day. By Jeremiah's time that promise had hardened into a guarantee that did not depend on faithfulness.
cultural:
Covering the head (verses 3 and 4) was a sign of grief and shame, as when David climbed the Mount of Olives with his head covered (2 Samuel 15:30). Public fasting, burnt offerings, and grain offerings (verse 12) were the ordinary ways Israel sought God in a national crisis, much as Joel 1 and 2 call for a fast in a time of locusts and drought. The shock of the chapter is that these right actions are refused. The problem is not the ritual but the hearts behind it: verse 10 says the people "love to wander" and have not held back their feet.

The images of verses 5 and 6 would have struck a first reader hard. The doe was known for tender care of her young, so a doe that abandons her newborn shows how extreme the drought had become. The prayer's titles for God also carry weight. "Hope of Israel" (verse 8) uses a word that can also mean a pool of water, a fitting double sense in a drought. The complaint that God is like "a traveler who stays but a night" accuses him of treating his own land like a roadside inn, and "a warrior powerless to save" throws at him the charge that he is failing to be what he claimed.
literary: The chapter is a liturgy of lament, like a service of prayer held in a crisis, but with God's replies inserted. Verses 2 to 6 describe the drought, moving from the city's nobles to the farmers to the wild animals. Verses 7 to 9 are a communal prayer of confession and appeal. Verses 10 to 16 are God's refusal, with a dialogue in which Jeremiah raises the matter of the other prophets. Verses 17 and 18 give the prophet's lament, and verses 19 to 22 are a second communal prayer, which ends not with an answer but with a confession of faith: only God sends rain. The refrain "sword and famine" (with plague in verse 12) repeats through the middle section and becomes a standard triad in Jeremiah. The two prayers mirror each other, both confessing sin and both appealing to God's name.

outline.t: The drought: city, field, and wilderness
A prayer of confession: do not forsake us
The prophets of peace and their end
The prophet's tears for his people
A second prayer: we put our hope in You

doctrines.note: The prayers of this chapter are models of honest lament: they confess sin, appeal to God's name and covenant, and even accuse him of acting like a stranger. God does not grant the request, but the prayers are preserved in Scripture, and the last one ends in hope.

The chapter distinguishes true prophecy from false. The false prophets speak "the futility and delusion of their own minds" and say what people want to hear; the test is whether God sent them, not whether the message comforts.
The closing verse confesses that rain does not come from idols or from the sky on its own but from God. Weather, harvest, and daily bread are gifts under his hand.
Fasting and sacrifice without turning of the heart are refused. The chapter separates repentance from its outward forms.

words.note: Miqveh, hope, from a root meaning to wait for. The same spelling is used elsewhere for a gathering of water, a pool (in later Judaism a miqveh became the name of the ritual bath). Calling God "Hope of Israel" in a drought quietly uses both senses: he is the one they wait for, and the source of the water they lack. Jeremiah uses the title again in 17:13, where the LORD is the fountain of living water.

Sheqer, falsehood, lie, deception. It is one of Jeremiah's key words (he uses it more than any other prophet), and here it describes the prophets "prophesying lies" in God's name. For Jeremiah the deepest lie is religious: a promise of peace spoken in God's name that God never gave.

Marpe, healing or remedy. In verse 19 the people complain that they are "beyond healing" and that they hoped for "the time of healing" but found terror. The word links the drought to Jeremiah's larger picture of a nation with a wound no one can cure except God (8:22; 30:17).

christ: The chapter's prayers ask God to act "for the sake of Your name" and to remember his covenant, and the New Testament's answer is that God did remember it in sending his Son (Luke 1:72). The link is the covenant story, not a direct prediction. Jeremiah's tears for "the virgin daughter of my people" anticipate Jesus weeping over Jerusalem, and his clash with prophets who cried peace where there was none foreshadows Jesus' warnings about false prophets who look harmless but are not (Matthew 7:15). The deepest link is the one the last prayer reaches for: the people had no hope but God himself, the "Hope of Israel". In the New Testament, Paul says he is in chains for the hope of Israel (Acts 28:20), meaning the promised Messiah and the resurrection, the answer to a need no ritual could meet.

hard.q: If God refuses the people's fasting and prayer, what hope is there for anyone who prays?
hard.a: The refusal can sound as though God shuts his ears to sincere prayer. But the chapter gives reasons. The people's prayer in verses 7 to 9 is a genuine confession in form, yet verse 10 says they still "love to wander", and their prophets were assuring them no disaster would come. The refusal is aimed at a nation that wanted rescue from consequences while holding on to what caused them. It is also a refusal to prevent a judgment already decided, not a refusal ever to hear. The same book promises that when the people seek God with all their heart in exile, they will find him (29:12-14). Many readers also notice that the chapter ends with the people still praying, and that Scripture keeps the prayer. Lament that receives no immediate answer is still addressed to someone.

questions: The people called God "a stranger in the land". Have you ever felt that God was distant in a crisis? What did you do with that feeling?
False prophets promised peace because people wanted to hear it. How can you tell the difference between comfort that is true and comfort that is only welcome?
The final prayer ends without an answer but with hope in God alone. What would it take to pray that way in a situation that isn't resolved?
